claims.text: What the image looks like Buzzword: bamboo spine on spine X-ray → ankylosing spondylitis
claims.quote: Bamboo spine Spine X-ray Ankylosing spondylitis

claims.text: Earliest radiograph abnormalities: pseudo-widening caused by subchondral erosions, followed by sclerosis or later narrowing and eventually fusion in the sacroiliac joints; changes are symmetric
claims.quote: The earliest abnormalities on radiographs are pseudo-widening caused by subchondral erosions, followed by sclerosis or later narrowing and eventually fusion in the sacroiliac joints. Changes are symmetric.

claims.text: Early spine changes: upper lumbar vertebral squaring with sclerosis at the corners (shiny corner sign), spotty ligamentous calcification, and 1 or 2 evolving syndesmophytes
claims.quote: Early changes in the spine are upper lumbar vertebral squaring with sclerosis at the corners (shiny corner sign), spotty ligamentous calcification, and 1 or 2 evolving syndesmophytes.

claims.text: Late changes: a “bamboo spine” appearance from prominent syndesmophytes, diffuse paraspinal ligamentous calcification, and osteoporosis; these changes develop in some patients on average over 10 years
claims.quote: Late changes result in a “bamboo spine” appearance, resulting from prominent syndesmophytes, diffuse paraspinal ligamentous calcification, and osteoporosis; these changes develop in some patients on average over 10 years.

claims.text: Example spine radiograph: extra bone (bright white) laid down between the vertebrae; in places this fusion is complete, giving the appearance of a "bamboo spine"
claims.quote: In this radiograph of the spine of a patient with ankylosing spondylitis, extra bone (bright white) has been laid down between the vertebrae. In places this fusion is complete, giving the appearance of a "bamboo spine."

claims.text: Example lateral cervical spine radiograph (severe, long-standing disease): a rigid cervical spine, completely ankylosed (“bamboo spine”) due to syndesmophytes, fused facet (apophyseal) joints, and paraspinal ligamentous calcification
claims.quote: This lateral view of the cervical spine shows a rigid cervical spine in a patient with severe, long-standing ankylosing spondylitis. The spine is completely ankylosed (“bamboo spine”) due to syndesmophytes, fused facet (apophyseal) joints, and paraspinal ligamentous calcification.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Typical changes may not become visible on radiographs for years; MRI shows changes earlier (early inflammatory changes, bone marrow edema on T2-weighted images with fatty changes, subtle structural abnormalities), but there is no consensus on its role in routine diagnosis; pelvic MRI should be done if suspicion of spondyloarthritis is high or other causes must be excluded; routine monitoring with serial spine radiographs is not recommended
claims.quote: Changes typical of ankylosing spondylitis may not become visible on radiographs for years. MRI shows changes earlier, but there is no consensus regarding its role in routine diagnosis given the lack of prospective, validated data in regard to its diagnostic utility. Pelvic MRI should be done if the index of suspicion of spondyloarthritis is high or if there is a need to exclude other causes of the patient's symptoms. MRI shows early inflammatory changes, bone marrow edema on T2-weighted images with fatty changes, and subtle structural abnormalities. Lastly, routine monitoring of radiographic changes with serial spine radiographs is not recommended.

claims.text: Labs: generally ESR, CRP, and CBC; HLA-B27 is present in 90% of White patients but also in up to 10% of the general population depending on ethnicity; no laboratory test is diagnostic; if still suspected, radiography or MRI of the lumbosacral spine and sacroiliac joints, where sacroiliitis on radiograph strongly supports the diagnosis
claims.quote: Patients should generally be tested with ESR, CRP, and complete blood count. Rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-anticyclic citrullinated peptide [CCP] antibodies, and antinuclear antibodies are needed only if peripheral arthritis suggests other diagnoses. The HLA-B27 allele is present in 90% of White patients with ankylosing spondylitis, but it is also present in up to 10% of the general population depending on ethnicity (1). No laboratory test is diagnostic, but results can increase suspicion for the disorder or exclude other disorders that can simulate ankylosing spondylitis. If, after these tests, ankylosing spondylitis is still suspected, patients should undergo radiography or MRI of the lumbosacral spine and sacroiliac joints; demonstration of sacroiliitis on radiograph strongly supports the diagnosis.

claims.text: Causes The prototypical spondyloarthropathy: a systemic disorder with inflammation of the axial skeleton, large peripheral joints, and digits; nocturnal back pain; morning back stiffness; accentuated kyphosis; constitutional symptoms; aortitis; cardiac conduction abnormalities; and anterior uveitis
claims.quote: Ankylosing spondylitis is the prototypical spondyloarthropathy and a systemic disorder characterized by inflammation of the axial skeleton, large peripheral joints, and digits; nocturnal back pain; morning back stiffness; accentuated kyphosis; constitutional symptoms; aortitis; cardiac conduction abnormalities; and anterior uveitis.

claims.text: 3 times more frequent in men than in women; begins most often between ages 20 and 40; 10 to 20 times more common among first-degree relatives; HLA-B27 present in 90% of White patients (and up to 10% of the general population, depending on ethnicity); identical-twin concordance only approximately 50%, suggesting environmental factors contribute
claims.quote: Ankylosing spondylitis is 3 times more frequent in men than in women and begins most often between ages 20 and 40. It is 10 to 20 times more common among first-degree relatives of patients with ankylosing spondylitis than in the general population. The human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) allele is present in 90% of White patients with ankylosing spondylitis (1), but it is also present in up to 10% of the general population depending on ethnicity. The risk of ankylosing spondylitis in first-degree relatives with the HLA-B27 allele is approximately 20%. Increased prevalence of HLA-B27 in White people or HLA-B7 in Black people supports a genetic predisposition. However, the concordance rate in identical twins is only approximately 50%, suggesting that environmental factors contribute.

claims.text: Symptoms Back pain (often nocturnal, of varying intensity) eventually becomes recurrent; morning stiffness (typically relieved by activity) and paraspinal muscle spasm develop; kyphosis is common in untreated patients; severe hip and shoulder arthritis can eventually develop; in late stages, untreated patients may develop accentuated kyphosis, loss of lumbar lordosis, and fixed bent-forward posturing; there may be peripheral joint involvement, sometimes dactylitis; Achilles and patellar tendinitis can occur
claims.quote: Back pain—often nocturnal and of varying intensity—eventually becomes recurrent. Morning stiffness, typically relieved by activity and paraspinal muscle spasm, develops. A flexed or bent-over posture eases back pain and paraspinal muscle spasm; thus, kyphosis is common in untreated patients. Severe hip and shoulder arthritis can eventually develop. In late stages, untreated patients may develop accentuated kyphosis, loss of lumbar lordosis, and fixed bent-forward posturing, with compromised pulmonary function and an inability to lie flat. There may be peripheral potentially deforming joint involvement, sometimes involving isolated digit diffuse swelling (dactylitis). Achilles and patellar tendinitis can occur.

claims.text: Systemic manifestations in approximately 25%: recurrent acute anterior uveitis is common; neurologic signs occasionally (compression radiculitis or sciatica, vertebral fracture or subluxation, cauda equina syndrome); cardiovascular: aortic insufficiency, aortitis, angina, pericarditis, and cardiac conduction abnormalities (which may be asymptomatic); nonspecific colitis has been noted in 30%
claims.quote: Systemic manifestations of ankylosing spondylitis occur in approximately 25% of patients (1). Recurrent, acute anterior uveitis is common; less commonly it becomes protracted and severe enough to impair vision. Neurologic signs occasionally result from compression radiculitis or sciatica, vertebral fracture or subluxation, or cauda equina syndrome. Cardiovascular manifestations include aortic insufficiency, aortitis, angina, pericarditis, and cardiac conduction abnormalities (which may be asymptomatic). Dyspnea, cough, or hemoptysis can rarely result from nontuberculous fibrosis or cavitation of an upper lobe of the lung; cavitary lesions can become secondarily infected with Aspergillus. Nonspecific colitis has been noted in 30% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis.

claims.text: Suspect in patients, particularly young men, with nocturnal back pain plus prolonged morning stiffness and kyphosis, diminished chest expansion, Achilles or patellar tendinitis, or unexplained anterior uveitis; a first-degree relative with ankylosing spondylitis should raise suspicion
claims.quote: Ankylosing spondylitis should be suspected in patients, particularly young men, with nocturnal back pain plus prolonged morning stiffness and kyphosis, diminished chest expansion, Achilles or patellar tendinitis, or unexplained anterior uveitis. A first-degree relative with ankylosing spondylitis should raise suspicion.

claims.text: Treatment and next step NSAIDs are first-line therapy for most patients: they reduce pain and suppress joint inflammation and muscle spasm, increasing range of motion; the dose should be as low as possible, but maximum doses may be needed with active disease
claims.quote: NSAIDs are first-line therapy for most patients. They reduce pain and suppress joint inflammation and muscle spasm, thereby increasing range of motion, which facilitates exercise and prevents contractures. Most NSAIDs work in ankylosing spondylitis, and tolerance and toxicity dictate drug choice. The daily dose of NSAIDs should be as low as possible, but maximum doses may be needed with active disease.

claims.text: Biologic therapy when NSAIDs give inadequate control: TNF inhibitors (eg, etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab) are often strikingly effective for inflammatory back pain; adalimumab or infliximab are preferred over etanercept with recurrent uveitis; if a TNF inhibitor is ineffective, switching to an IL-17 inhibitor is preferred to another TNF inhibitor
claims.quote: Biologic therapy should be initiated when patients have inadequate disease control with NSAIDs. TNF inhibitors (eg, etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab) are often strikingly effective for inflammatory back pain. Adalimumab or infliximab are preferred over etanercept for the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis in patients with recurrent uveitis. For patients in whom a TNF inhibitor is ineffective, switching to an IL-17 inhibitor is preferred to switching to another TNF inhibitor.

claims.text: Use TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, or JAK inhibitors in patients who respond inadequately to NSAIDs
claims.quote: Use tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, interleukin-17 (IL-17) inhibitors, or Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors in patients who respond inadequately to NSAIDs.

claims.text: Daily exercise and supportive measures (eg, postural training, therapeutic exercise) are vital, strengthening the extensor rather than flexor muscles; smoking cessation should be encouraged (associated with increased pain and disease activity)
claims.quote: For proper posture and joint motion, daily exercise and other supportive measures (eg, postural training, therapeutic exercise) are vital to strengthen muscle groups that oppose the direction of potential deformities (ie, the extensor rather than flexor muscles). Reading while lying prone and pushing up on the elbows or pillows and thus extending the back may help keep the back flexible. Smoking cessation should also be encouraged because it is associated with increased pain and disease activity (3).
